#6800. Why El Clasico Is the Best Grudge Match in All of Sports

Last Saturday, before the biggest grudge match in international soccer, Spanish police officers decked out in riot gear surrounded my Barcelona hotel. Blue lights bounced from the sun-stained stone of the alley as kids scrambled away in the distance. In the skirmish, one had lost a single ASICS sneaker that sat idly in the road until, sometime between night and the light of day, someone snatched it up for themselves. You often hear of the way heated football rivalries and cup finals bring out a kind of mob mentality among fans. The match, however, wasn’t set to kick off for another 24 hours.

Three days prior I’d landed in Barcelona to attend FC Barcelona versus Real Madrid, better known as El Clásico, for which Tyler the Creator’s GOLF brand had partnered with Spotify on Barcelona’s gameday kits. If you care about football in the slightest you know about El Clásico, though it’s worth knowing about even if you don’t.

Since 1902—the year of Real Madrid’s founding, and three years after that of FC Barcelona—the two biggest football clubs in Spain have clashed in a rivalry match dubbed El Clásico (the face-off now happens twice a season, plus various tournament play that varies in schedule year to year). Before last week’s installment, the match had been played 264 times over 122 years. In most high-stakes football rivalries, one club holds a historical edge: Arsenal has a handy 20 to 30 wins over Tottenham Hotspur in the North London Derby, depending on when you start keeping track, while Manchester United edges out Liverpool in total wins. But heading into the first El Clásico of the 2026-27 La Liga season, Barcelona and Real Madrid stood deadlocked with 106 wins each.

American sports rivalries are often the result of proximity, with most pitting divisional neighbors and crosstown rivals against one another, with the exception of teams that share a bitter history of championship bouts (like the Lakers and the Celtics). But if we’re being honest, not even Yankees-Red Sox holds a candle to El Clásico. Apart from both competing in the upper echelon of La Liga’s clubs, FC Barcelona and Real Madrid’s rivalry has stewed in over a century of political turmoil between the Catalan capital and the city that houses the Spanish throne. During the 20th century as Spain looked to enforce a uniform identity across the nation, Catalonia sought to maintain its independence from the crown and, crucially, its right to speak Catalan rather than Spanish. Francisco Franco’s dictatorship brought more enmity, as Madrid became the proxy club for a centralized Spain while Barcelona came to represent Catalonia’s Republican Left. During the Franco years, when both the language and the flag of Catalan were banned, Barcelona’s Camp Nou stadium became a safe haven for the free expression of Catalan identity. Meanwhile, Franco’s foreign minister Fernando Maria de Castiella declared Real Madrid “the best embassy we’ve ever had.” The wounds of that era have hardly subsided: while the war may be over, as recently as 2017 the Catalan people voted on whether or not they’d remain a part of Spain (the vote was declared illegal by the Spanish government, and there was police intervention at polling stations).

Today, the clubs are recognized as polar opposites in every sense, from politics to style of play: Real Madrid stands for conservatism and a unified Spain, while Barcelona remains the club of the rebellious Left. Madrid takes an Evil Empire approach to roster construction, buying up the most exciting free agents on the market for record-breaking fees. (This century alone they’ve rostered Cristiano Ronaldo, David Beckham, and Zinedine Zidane, and the club currently boasts a striker line that includes Jude Bellingham, Kylian Mbappé, and Vinicius Jr.) Barcelona, on the other hand, has the most acclaimed and successful youth academy in all of football. The school, La Masia, has promoted a singular theory of football for decades, prioritizing position play and a dominant possession game perfected by FC Barcelona veterans like Lionel Messi, Xavi, Pep Guardiola, and Andrés Iniesta. When Spain won the World Cup this summer, they did so with eight former students of La Masia on the pitch (one of whom, Marc Cucarella, currently plays for Real Madrid).

To this day, the rivalry is characterized by an unmistakable hostility. In my four days in Barcelona, I didn’t see one person wearing Real Madrid’s crest, though the souvenir shops lining La Rambla were well-stocked with the club’s bootleg gear. At one point, I walked past a wall scrawled with graffiti: “SPANISH GO HOME.” When we finally got to the match, most Madrid fans were sequestered to a supporter section in the upper deck surrounded by protective plexiglass.

“This is the biggest match in club football,” explained Joel Jaggar, a British transplant who’s lived in Barcelona for a decade. Jaggar runs Real Vintage Football, a rare jersey boutique in El Raval (just outside of the city’s Gothic Quarter) that was unsurprisingly overwhelmed with visitors all weekend. He’d stocked up on at least a hundred Messi jerseys, all of which were gone by the time they closed on Friday. “A lot of people come to Barcelona specifically for this game,” he shared. “Big fans, sure, but also people who want to experience the game for the sake of the experience.” Globally, he argued, the word “Barcelona” is as closely associated with the club as it is the city. “You can’t say the same for Madrid,” he quipped.

Jaggar and I met the morning after a swell of student-organized protests regarding the city’s cost-of-living crisis boiled over into vandalism and looting near the neighborhood that houses his store. There was even suspicion El Clásico would have to be postponed or cancelled altogether. Come morning though, those anxieties had faded–as is so often the case, football continued uninterrupted.

Even with capacity capped at around 62,000 during ongoing renovations, Camp Nou is something to behold. Ahead of kickoff, supporters lifted color-coordinated pieces of poster nestled into each seat,forming a massive, stadium-wide tifo in the colors of the club and, in our section, the Catalonian flag. Fireworks exploded, and El Clásico began.

But much of the match’s first half was mired in tension, as Barcelona dominated possession but failed to score. The crowd finally began to pop when Madrid nabbed their first goal, then properly exploded when Barca tied it up in the second half. When Mbappé scored his second goal of the evening at ‘87 minutes after a beautiful assist from Bellingham, he vaulted over to the gate of the Barcelona supporters’ section, taunting them as trash thrown from the crowd rained over him. Madrid held on, gaining the tiniest of advantages in the El Clásico win count: 107 to their rivals’ 106.

As we walked out of Camp Nou, which will hold a whopping 105,000 spectators when its renovation is complete, I thought about the sort of sporting events that tend to grace bucket lists: Super Bowls and World Cup Finals and World Series games. So often the point is the spectacle of a season or tournament ending—the big trophy, the championship ring, the confetti and fireworks. El Clásico is different. There’s no trophy at the end, no ultimate resolution. Like the ideological divide for which it’s become a proxy, El Clásico is in a constant state of ebb and flow. Each time Barcelona and Real Madrid take the pitch, there’s no decisive victory so much as another brick laid in the foundation of football’s greatest rivalry. These clubs have come to blows 265 times. But as long as there are football stadiums in Barcelona and Madrid, El Clásico will endure as a conduit for the enduring rancor between the country's two biggest cities.

As the host of last night’s 2026 CFDA Awards in New York City, all eyes were on Keke Palmer to deliver us a major fashion moment. The annual awards ceremony, after all, is all about celebrating American style and design. “Fashion is such a big part of how I tell stories, so getting to celebrate the people behind it was exciting,” Palmer tells Vogue today, post-CFDAs. “I love how a look can connect different eras, and bring a memory or a feeling into the present. To be in a room celebrating that creativity, while bringing my own personality and humor to the evening, felt like a beautiful fit.”

Of course, Palmer did not disappoint on that front. The star went archival for the night—as she is wont to do—bringing four vintage gems to the red carpet. “I wanted my looks to be unique, and celebrate some incredible talent from the past,” says Palmer of her fashion direction. “Everything with me is somehow a throwback or referential. That’s part of the kind of artist I am: Fashion becomes another way to tell that pop culture story.”

Working with stylist Molly Dickson, the duo wanted each of the four looks to have its own moment throughout the night. Palmer first hit the red carpet in a one-of-a-kind (and incredibly rare) Bob Mackie piece from the 1970s. The dress has a particularly noteworthy history: The strappy, shimmery-gold gown was originally custom-made for actor and singer Raquel Welch, which she wore to perform “I’m a Woman” alongside Cher on The Cher Show back in 1975. (You’ve all seen the clip.) “Wearing Bob Mackie was one of the first ideas I mentioned to Molly,” says Palmer. “His work holds so much entertainment history, and I loved being able to bring my own energy to a piece with that story. It’s classic, and it felt like the right way to step into the night.”

Turns out, the iconic piece of pop culture was sourced from the professional vintage dealer Timeless Vixen—a celebrity favorite that Sabrina Carpenter and Kylie Jenner also use for their extremely rare red carpet pulls. “When Keke’s styling team reached out looking for something special by Bob Mackie, this piece immediately came to mind,” says owner Lauren Lepire. “I’ve always adored his work, and with his recent passing, it’s especially meaningful to see Keke bring such an iconic design back into the spotlight.”

From there, Palmer then changed into her three other vintage frocks of the night. There was the black skin-revealing Marc Bouwer dress once worn by Toni Braxton; a striped, one-shouldered 1980s Halston number; And a slinky black 1970s Stephen Burrows to end with a bang. “For me, it was a story through the ages, celebrating these designers and the women who brought their clothes to life,” says Palmer. “We also told a black and gold color story, ending with a look that brought the two together. That sense of integration feels very connected to where I am artistically—bringing different references and parts of myself into one expression.”

While playing dress up was undoubtedly a highlight of the night for Palmer, her favorite moments included some unexpected run-ins with fellow stars. “You’re doing a show, but you also get to connect with people whose work you admire and enjoy being in the room together,” says Palmer. “I loved seeing Demi Moore backstage in between moments, seeing Law Roach, and catching up with Prabal Gurung. Those little moments in between everything are some of my favorites. Saw my girl Brandy, too!”

After delivering her statement fashions at the CFDAs, Palmer says she ended the night with one thing: “Bed! I’m a homebody.” Up next? She will be filming season two of The ’Burbs, and working on new music, too. (She just released her last video, “Keke Frankenstein,” this Halloween weekend.) “I’m building the world around my album, and having so much fun with ‘Keke Frankenstein,’” says Palmer. “I love when the music, visuals, fashion, and characters can all speak to one another.”

In other words: Palmer stays booked and busy. “Between motherhood, music, acting, and building Practice by Palmer, there’s always something happening,” says Palmer. “This fall, I’ve been making room for experiences that feed me as a person. The ‘play’ in me still has a way of becoming productive. #Virgo!”

#6797. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#6794. 31 Best Gifts for Mom in 2026, According to GQ Editors

There's an art to giving a good gift to someone who's been a mother to you, whether that's your actual mom, grandmother, or the person who's always looked out for you. And it has precious little to do with how much you spend. They say what goes around comes around, and when the occasion comes to buy her something special, there's not better time to return a little of the favor. To that end, we've rounded up the best gifts for mom, from modest indulgences to proper splurges, all chosen with an eye toward good taste, a little surprise, and the small triumph of getting it just right.

Still stumped? We'd suggest perusing the rest of our gift guides and signing up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

I have an AYR sweater in this very fabric, and I've been wearing the hell out of it lately. It's extraordinarily soft, with a bouncy, bouclé-like texture that you really have to feel to appreciate. The High has all that going for it, plus a cropped fit and a prim, high-set collar.

We're firm believers that a good tuxedo is one you'd wear any old day. Which is why we're digging this casual cotton tuxedo shirt from Gap's collaboration with Victoria Beckham. It's awfully chic, and a reason for her to get "dressed up" with nowhere special to go.

Breda's Jane Time Charm is a clever little thing. Made from gold-plated stainless steel, the miniature timepiece can be worn as a necklace or clipped to a keychain, but I think it makes for a pretty decoration on a lapel.

Timex's Cavatina Mini looks like something you'd stumble upon at an estate sale, with its petite 17mm case and old-school script logo. The design nods to the brand's '60s-era women's watches, though this one's fresh out of the box.

Thistles is an IYKYK eyewear label whose fashionable milieu stretches from Em Rata to Kim Gordon and any mom worth her vintage Prada. There are plenty of excellent frames to choose from, but the square-shaped Suede is a safe bet.

Coach has a bona fide can't-miss gift on its hands with the Brooklyn, a slouchy, do-it-all carryall. It comes in a range of sizes, but we're partial to the 34, a generously proportioned everyday bag with room for just about everything.

Cashmere is the safest bet you can make at Quince, so it's nice to see the brand putting it to work as the lining of these leather gloves. And at that price, there isn't much to complain about.

If she's made it this far in life without a pair of UGGs, the Zora ballet flat might be the one that finally wins her over. And if she's already living that UGG life, well, she's gonna need these.

A fresher, more spirited take on the original Coco, Coco Mademoiselle pairs sparkling orange and jasmine with rose and patchouli. For a mom with a taste for the classics, but an appreciation for modern flair, this one'll hit.

We recommended Therabody's Depuffing Wand last year, and we're running it back because it's just so dang good at what it does. Hot and cold treatments in one wonderfully unfussy little device make it a welcome addition to her skincare routine.

I like giving silk pillowcases because they're a beauty treatment and a bedroom upgrade in one. Clementine's smooth silk helps reduce friction against hair, minimizing tangles and breakage, while leaving fewer sleep creases.

Dyson's new travel-size Supersonic brings the brand's high-powered drying technology to a more portable package. It's compact enough to tuck into a carry-on without sacrificing the elite airflow of the original, and it's compatible with all the same attachments.

Laneige's Lip Sleeping Mask is a cult favorite, and chances are she already knows it, maybe even swears by it. But the new gingerbread flavor for the season? A stroke of seasonal madness, and a nice little stocking stuffer to boot.

Aesop is about as close to a sure thing as gifting gets. Its new Solias Hand Serum has a light, floral, citrusy, and herbaceous aroma, with a nourishing formula to help keep Mom's hands in fighting shape through winter.

No. 04 Bois de Balincourt has long drawn comparisons to Le Labo's Santal 33, only at a considerably friendlier price and without the burdern of its own ubiquity. Warm sandalwood and cedar, with earthy vetiver and a little spice—a perfect year-round candle.

I'm a coffee drinker through and through, but I'd consider switching allegiances to tea if it meant getting to use this teapot from Balmuda. Just looking at the thing feels therapeutic.

For farmers' market queens, this tote really does tick all the boxes: heavy-duty cotton canvas, six exterior pockets, a clever strap for securing, say, a bouquet of dahlihas, and a structured design that stands upright on its own.

This insulated Dutch oven tote from Staub and Clare V. is just the thing for the potluck monarch arriving with a cassoulet in tow. A highly specific gifting proposition, admittedly, but an excellent one nonetheless.

Inspired by the pleated designs of Issey Miyake, Wooj's Kinoko lamp has a pretty mushroom silhouette and a softly ribbed shade. A charming little thing for that neglected corner that could use some illumination.

There are plenty of newfangled brands making cute, colorful homewares these days, but long live Marimekko. These towels caught my eye for their classic brick pattern, rendered in a perfect shade of red, with all the pedigree of Finnish design behind them.

Apple's new entry-level laptop might be marketed to students, but it's also a very good laptop for anyone who just needs to do regular laptop things. Browsing, emailing, streaming, the occasional spreadsheet—the Neo handles the everyday stuff without demanding a small fortune for the privilege of owning a fruit-embossed gadget.

If you really want to round out the gift, throw in this laptop sleeve from Cuyana. Made from Italian leather, it's chic enough to be carried around on its own, which is more than you can say for most laptop accessories.

Sony's XM6 headphones are already among the best noise-canceling cans you can buy, but now they come in this very, very good matte olive gray colorway. As if we needed another reason to recommend them.

Brooklyn-based designer Virginia Sin made a name for herself with porcelain versions of disposable paper plates, and her talent for making everyday objects feel a little more special extends beyond the dinner table. Case in point: this little number, which would look mighty fine on mom's desk.

Twelve South's Valet gives her phone a proper place to recharge, with a handy catchall for keys, jewelry, and whatever else tends to accumulate around the house.

Prettier humidifiers? There aren't many. Canopy's 2.0 is a welcome antidote to the moisture-sapping misery of winter, and will look great wherever she puts it.

And just like that, aesthetically pleasing pill organizers are a thing. Fine by us. Where else is she supposed to stash her daily rotation of vitamins, supplements, and what have you?

For the mom who likes to get her miles in, these open-ear headphones let her soundtrack a morning run without losing track of the world around her. They're lightweight, stay put even when she's picking up the pace, and pack up to 12 hours of battery life.

#6793. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#6790. Haley Stevens, Elizabeth Holmes, and the Limits We Place on Female Agency

I haven’t been able to stop thinking about Elizabeth Holmes—her documented crimes, her relationships with male narcissists—since seeing the bizarre performance of innocence she puts on in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary You Can See Everything. But over the weekend, as I watched Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens withdraw her endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, to instead back his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in the midterms, I couldn’t help spotting a parallel in their stories.

Amid the left’s backlash against Stevens, whose fallout with El-Sayed hinged, in part, on their opposing views on Israel, several people in her life have cited her attorney fiancé, Jason Turkish, as an influence on her campaign. A former spokesperson of Stevens’s, Caitlin Legacki, argued on X that Turkish—a prominent Jewish Democratic fund-raiser who announced his support for Rogers over El-Sayed before Stevens did—was “vaporizing Haley’s future so that he can be a main character in this moment and it is sad to watch her participate in that.” She went on to claim that Turkish “was an extraordinarily toxic presence, was verbally abusive to staff, and had some of the worst political instincts I’ve ever witnessed.” Other former campaign staffers have spoken out about Turkish allegedly sending Stevens negative social media posts about herself. “He would wind her up, and then we’d have to wind her down,” one aide said.

A somewhat similar narrative emerged from You Can See Everything, in which Holmes’s fiancé, Billy Evans, appears to exert control over everything from the couple’s finances to Holmes’s social media presence and even the way she beats eggs. (In comments posted to X earlier today, Evans, asked if there was “one misconception from the film” that he wanted to address, replied, in part: “That I somehow control Liz. Anyone who actually knows her would find that idea hilarious. She's fiercely independent, strongwilled, and my best friend.”)

Yet to frame either woman as a useful idiot to her corrupting, controlling partner is not only facile, but somewhat misogynistic. Certainly, in Holmes’s case, it is possible for a criminally manipulative person to herself be manipulated. To blame Stevens’s fiancé for her “betrayal” of the Democratic Party, meanwhile, would be to call into question the agency of a woman who has served in the House of Representatives for the last seven years.

Is our cultural perception of womanhood still so narrow that when we see a public figure transgress or step out of line, we question if it really could have been of her own volition? As Stevens put it in a statement posted to X on Monday: “A woman can serve in Congress, run statewide, and fight for her convictions, and still be told that when she makes a choice people dislike, someone else must be pulling the strings. That is sexism dressed up as political analysis.”

She added: “My fiancé has his own views. I have mine. I made this decision, and I am proud of it. Do not question my independence simply because you disagree with my conclusion.”

The world would be a much simpler place if all inventors were honest and all politicians were loyal to their parties. But given that’s not the case, maybe we can use this cultural moment to gut-check the way we perceive women in the public eye. As The Other Two’s Brooke Dubek—a TV character partially based on a female creator whose own professional conduct was reported to be questionable, at best—chants defiantly while sitting on a feminist panel: “Women can suck.”

#6789. What Writing a Book About JFK Jr. Taught Me About Personal Style

John F. Kennedy Jr. wasn’t the first guy to ride a bike wearing a suit. Likewise, the presidential scion and People’s 1988 Sexiest Man Alive didn’t invent the backward Kangol cap, the pinstriped suit, or wearing a waistcoat with jeans—he just did it better than pretty much anybody else. That’s a big part of why he was one of the most photographed men on the planet in the 1990s, and why he remains a menswear moodboard staple today, nearly 30 years after his untimely death. Still, no matter how hard you try, and no matter how closely you hew to the source material, all attempts to replicate JFK Jr.’s style are destined to leave you looking like a runner-up in a Washington Square Park lookalike contest.

Ask anyone who encountered John-John in his prime—which, in my experience, is virtually everyone who lived in Manhattan in the 1990s—and the first thing they’ll mention is his magnetism, his charm, and the fact that, against all odds, he was actually better-looking in person. I know this because, having recently written a book about JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve spent a good part of the last year poring over photos, reading biographies, speaking to people who knew him, and otherwise immersing myself in his world. Among the conclusions I’ve come to is that you probably won’t look as cool as JFK Jr. did wearing rollerblades, but there are a few style moves you can borrow from his playbook without resorting to full Kennedy cosplay.

JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was built on four pillars: tailoring, preppy basics, workwear, and sportswear. But it was the idiosyncratic way he combined them (i.e., a backward baseball cap with a suit, a polo neck sweater under a tweed blazer, hiking boots with tailored trousers) that resulted in some of his most memorable looks. Surprisingly, while the combination of straight-leg jeans, a button-up dress shirt, and a blazer has become shorthand for JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve never seen any evidence of him wearing it. In fact, he seldom wore jeans at all (some speculate his mother thought they looked shabby, while others told me that jeans didn’t complement his active lifestyle). That said, plenty of other ’90s style icons, from Ralph Lauren to Jerry Seinfeld, rocked this particular look, and it’s a pretty easy one to pull off. As with everything about JFK Jr.’s style, it’s not about lifting these combinations wholesale, but understanding the precise balance of contrast that makes them work.

One of the most consistent elements of JFK Jr.’s style was his love of discordant accessories, from his collection of flat caps to his ever-present wallet chain to his Oakley Eye Jacket shades. Some of these were practical—he was so prone to misplacing his wallet and keys that he needed to chain them to his pants—but others reflected his love of color (funky knit caps), his enthusiasm for skiing (fleece headbands), and his passion for travel (various hats picked up on trips to India and Thailand). Some accessories will suit you better than others, but if you have a personal connection to it, all the better. And most importantly, limit yourself to one standout add-on per outfit.

Speaking of accessories: JFK Jr. was a dedicated scarf guy, and he’d pair one with everything from joggers and sneakers to his best navy blue suit. Rather than draping a scarf loosely around his neck, he tended to tie it in either a dressy overhand or classic Parisian knot, both of which lend a more formal look. He also loved wearing a thick scarf as outerwear, throwing it over a sweatshirt on a chilly day instead of a coat, often paired with a knit cap. For best results, don’t pick a scarf that matches the rest of your outfit too closely.

Among the most surprising things I discovered about JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was his watch collection. I wasn’t able to uncover any evidence of him wearing the long-lost Rolex Daytona given to him by Aristotle Onassis (a watch that, if ever found, would give Paul Newman a run for his money), but I did identify an unusually wide range of other pieces in his collection, from a Victorinox Swiss Army field watch to a Swatch chronograph to a vintage Rolex Oyster Perpetual. This is of a piece with everything else we know about JFK Jr.: he wasn’t bound by any single style, brand, or price point, and got just as much enjoyment out of a cheap quartz watch as a luxury mechanical one.

As a rich kid raised on the Upper East Side, JFK Jr.’s closet included plenty of blazers, chinos, and polos. He was a gym rat who loved playing sports, so he also had a lot of sweats, tees, and sneakers. He was a downtown socialite, so he owned a lot of nice suits and tuxes, too. He also had an enviable collection of graphic tees from NYC institutions like the Russian & Turkish Baths in the East Village and the New York Athletic Club, as well as some commemorating events like the 1984 NYC Fresh Festival, a seminal moment in hip-hop history. What stands out to me—and what I believe makes his style so distinctive—is that JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was an authentic reflection of who he was, where he came from, and what he loved. This might be the most important style lesson any of us can learn from him: Great personal style is less about clothes than wearing them in a way that expresses your individuality.

#6788. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

#6786. Dia Art Foundation and Chanel Reunited for the Fall Gala Honoring Steve McQueen and Roni Horn

On Monday evening, the four blocks between Dia Chelsea on West 22nd Street and the nearby Storied NYC event space proved to be a runway of their own. After taking in an exhibit of work by Argentine artist David Lamelas at the industrial space, some 400 guests made their way over to a cocktail reception and elegant candlelit dinner in support of Dia Art Foundation.

Chanel’s creative director Matthieu Blazy had flown in specially to co-chair the nonprofit’s annual Fall Night event, alongside contemporary artists Carrie Mae Weems and Rosemarie Trockel. The evening’s honorees, British artist and filmmaker Steve McQueen and New York-born writer and artist Roni Horn, were the toast of the room—with the likes of Sofia Coppola and Marion Cotillard turning out to raise a glass.

From the stage, artist Matthew Barney gave a poignant tribute to his longtime friend Horn. “I’ve never asked Roni if it was her, in the clown costume, in her photographic series Clowd and Cloun,” he said. “I guess I didn’t ask because I know that Roni isn’t a clown, but there is a brilliant comedian in there. And a poet, a pragmatist, an intimate, an analyst, a confidante, an artist, and a close friend—brutally funny, and awfully clear.”

Later in the evening, an homage to McQueen came via a surprise spoken-word and roving performance woven in between the room’s long candle-laden tables, courtesy of musician and poet Meshell Ndegeocello.

While it’s early days in the blossoming partnership between Chanel and Dia Art Foundation—Monday night’s festivities marking their second collaboration—it was the end of an era for Jessica Morgan. After 12 years, the director is moving across the pond to take up the reins as the director of Tate in London.

“It’s been an immense pleasure to stay true to our vision and mission,” she said, beaming. “I am most proud of the work that we’ve done with the collection. It has been a real transformation. We inherited an amazing body of work from extraordinary artists collected in depth—but since then, we’ve tripled the collection by bringing in so many incredible voices, many of whom are here tonight.”

Over a dinner of braised short rib, attendees also heard remarks from board chair Nathalie de Gunzburg, who took special care to bid adieu to Morgan. “I have learned so much from you. Not only about this institution, but buildings, programming, conservation, HVAC, and gardening—but also as a woman, you are exceptional.” At her mention of all things construction-related, the crowd tittered, knowing full well the extent to which keeping Dia’s 12 locations and sites up and running and constantly installing ambitious multidisciplinary works remains a Herculean effort.

As a parting note, Morgan proudly revealed that Dia is nearing its $200 million endowment goal. “It’s been an absolute joy to work here,” she said, adding with a laugh: “I’m going to be looking very carefully to see what’s going on, so don’t mess it up.”

Alex McQueen, Steve McQueen and Jessica Morgan

Kim Yao, Matilde Guidelli Guidi and Jean-Gabriel Neukomm

#6784. 14 Best Work Jackets for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

For better or worse, the best work jackets for men are no longer associated with garages, factory floors, and loading docks. Instead, as the likes of Paul Mescal and Austin Butler (who told GQ he wore his for a year straight) continue to fly their flag, a great work jacket has become every guy's fastest route to semi-rugged heartthrob style.

Honestly, they make looking good almost too easy. First, they inject your fits with casual, weekend tough-guy energy. (This, to be clear, is a plus.) Second, they flatter you in all the right places, framing your shoulders and neatening up your waistline whether you’re pairing them with jeans or the kinds of wide, puddling trousers we've long been yapping about.

Better still, you don’t have to spend a fortune. The classics from Dickies and Carhartt are as dependable as ever, and even the independent designer options are within reach of your budget—this is a cotton-forward option, after all. Here are 14 of our favorites, all of which will only look better after a few years (and a few scuffs) of real wear.

The Carhartt Detroit work jacket is the classic for a reason. It’s been around for more than 70 years—not quite as old as blue jeans or cowboy boots, but easily in the upper echelon of American fashion’s great exports. So much so that today, luxury brands are riffing on it, even selling pre-distressed, washed-down versions at triple the price. (And yes, this is also the work jacket that Austin Butler told us he wears.)

Cut to the waist, and built from thick, stiff canvas with three perfectly placed front pockets, the Detroit is an Eisenhower-style silhouette (during WWII, the then-Army General overhauled U.S. military dress and introduced the cropped, boxy jacket to American forces). Its insulated blanket lining and corduroy collar also make it one of the few true year-round, toasty work jackets out there. Simply put, this is a real piece of clothing for real life. (Though if it's not fancy enough for you, there’s always the street-ready, slimmer, unlined Carhartt WIP version.)

Just like Dickies' iconic 874 work pants, the brand's insulated Eisenhower jacket (there he is again) is a hard-wearing, warm, wallet-friendly piece of gear that fits incredibly well. Nearly as old as the Detroit Jacket above, it doesn’t always get the same respect. But maybe that's just because it flies a little more under the radar, with its logo patch tucked discreetly near the hem. Decades in, it remains a low-key, low-cost icon—less shouty than its Carhartt cousin, but every bit as authentic.

Wallace & Barnes, J.Crew's workwear line, is back with tough fabrics, heritage details, and a big hit of #menswear-era nostalgia—and this wool-lined work jacket shows exactly why folks missed it so much. It has all of the heartthrob-coded details you probably had in mind when you decided to look for a jacket like this: Corduroy collar, zippered chest pocket, slightly cropped fit. But it isn't just good-looking. It also has a wool-blend blanket lining, for superior warmth to help you enjoy it even if the depths of winter. And that, if cost-per-wear logic still applies, makes it more than worth its slightly higher price point.

Welcome to the world of truly warm fabrics, and actually glove-friendly pockets. Filson’s been mastering cold-weather gear since your great-great-grandfather was in short pants, and this work jacket continues that legacy. Based on the brand’s original 1914 Cruiser, it’s cut from 24-ounce Mackinaw wool — a tightly woven twill that truly blocks wind, sheds rain, and stays warm even when wet. Without being mean, it’s built to outlast even you. Pricey? Sure. But it’s the kind of thing your kids will remember you by (and fight for) someday.

Buck Mason’s archive is full to bursting with vintage pieces from decades past, which explains why its collections are filled with absolute bangers these days. Here the brand has taken a mid-century work jacket and remade it, tweaking the fit to make it a touch more relaxed, and using a soft Italian doeskin cotton fabric that’s more plush than anything a worksite would have issued back in the day. There's even more to love in the details: Shoulder pleats for easy movement, real horn buttons on the chest pockets, and a dressy point collar.

For Lo-heads, Polo Ralph Lauren's hard-wearing zipper jackets are the stuff of legend. And while you might have grown up with an inherited cotton example from your dad, in the last decade of so, Polo has been pushing its ‘Bi-Swing’ polyester and/or nylon takes instead. That's fine, but some of us aren't so willing to trade in the soft, rugged comfort of a full-cotton jacket. That's where the rarer Bayport Poplin jacket comes in. A work jacket with no delusions, it’s not stealing the working man’s valor — it knows exactly what it is. It’s Ralph Lauren, and it knows you’re working hard at hardly working. But it's also strong enough to handle whatever activities you throw at it, leisure or otherwise.

Sure, Copenhagen's Mfpen has its silhouettes dialed, but don't overlook its fabrications. Here, it’s a dense wool-blend with a multi-tonal yarn construction. Textured, substantive, perfect.

While most waxed cotton jackets lean more country estate than work site, Tom Beckbe's high-quality range include a few closer, more modern fits. Perfect for those looking for a work jacket that's also waterproof.

A designer-adjacent example for the fashion crowd, this piece from South Korea's FrizmWORKS doesn't just look good, it feels good too, thanks to that soft leather collar that's just buttery once it's flipped up.

Stan Ray is part of what you might call the big three of American workwear, alongside Dickies and Carhartt). The Texas-born brand’s aptly named Roughneck Jacket delivers exactly what you’d expect. It’s tough, practical, and built for wear. Ribbed cuffs keep the cold out, while the washed-out hue delivers a perfectly broken-in look from day one.

This jacket from New York's Corridor—made from a hefty cotton-blend twill—is a more colorful take on the work jacket, and bound to give any fall fit a lift.

Just as the Polo jacket above is an RL icon, so is this faithfully-recreated nautical deck jacket from Ralph's RRL line. It's restocked every fall, it sells out every fall.

A key feature of all work jackets is their shorter length, but for those of us who want to make sure ours hits right at the belt, look no further than Abercrombie’s entry.

A leading Parisian purveyor of vintage garms, BRUT has recently moved into making its own stuff, all rooted in the archival vintage styles they obsess over. The results are, how you say, on point.

These days, work jackets seem to have an undeniable stranglehold on the imagination of guys who spend all day staring at their keyboards. (There’s a political element to this, of course. Whether or not you act in solidarity with your fellow laborers under capitalism, a work jacket allows you to look the part of the everyman.) But also, they’re just a great jacket for busy lives! There’s a generally accommodating cut that doesn’t restrict your movement, plenty of pockets, and hardy materials that can easily handle a snag, or sudden shower.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6781. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

My hair has never been bleached, so for a long time I didn’t think of it really could be damaged. Truthfully, I had been underestimating what this rarely-skipped step can do in our routine. The humble conditioner has also gotten a lot smarter. The bond builders and peptides that used to be reserved for salon treatments now show up in everyday formulas, along with proteins designed to mimic your hair’s own keratin. And, better yet, some of the best ones cost less than a blowout. Ahead, a handful of conditioners that myself, hairstylists, and trichologists recommend for damaged hair.

#6779. The Real-Life Diet of John King, Who Hides Mini Protein Bars Behind the Magic Wall on Election Night

Nobody white knuckles Election Day the way John King does. Since 2008, CNN’s chief national correspondent has spent his midterm and presidential elections in wizard-like command of the Magic Wall—the omnipresent interactive map that drills into granular data from county to county as votes trickle in. (This year it will also include stats that show whether the cost of gas, rent, or groceries have increased or decreased in specific precincts.) The so-called charthrob has also completed some especially long shifts—working back-to-back 12- to 16-hour days during the 2020 presidential election, when results took about a week to tabulate. This year, to prepare for the midterms, he’s been traveling nonstop between battleground states, interviewing sources to stay on top of the national mood. “The way to be at my best on election night is to actually do the homework by visiting those places in the year and a half or so leading up to the election,” he says.

That is no easy task, given the 63-year-old dad of three also lives with multiple sclerosis. To keep his symptoms in check and his head cool as results pour in, he’s created a disciplined regime that includes hitting the gym no matter how little sleep he gets, keeping a mental map of healthy places to eat in flyover country, and occasionally giving himself time to sightsee—or stare at a wall. GQ spoke with King a week ahead of Tuesday’s races to learn how he keeps steady amid the chaos.

John King: All this year, I’ve been on the road, on average, about two weeks a month for the midterm cycle. And we started obviously late last year. You have to do that. This last week is particularly grueling. Normally we go out and we do one state and we travel into say, North Carolina. We were there for three days. We went to Texas and we were there for four days, three nights. The schedule’s pretty busy on those days, but you have a little bit of breathing room and you can make time for a hotel gym and you can search a little bit to find a better restaurant that might have a few actual salads or fresh fish on the menu. This week, we’re doing five states in five days.

That included working until about 10 o’clock on Monday night and then having to catch a 6 a.m. flight Tuesday morning. It included last night wrapping at about 8 o’clock in Detroit and having to drive four, four and a half hours into central Ohio to be here today. On those days, you’re not really in control of your schedule. Your schedule is in charge of you. You just have to be somewhere at a certain point the next day. So everything is driven by that.

So can you fly there? If not, you have to drive there. And in those situations, if you’re talking about trying to keep a healthy diet, that becomes a pretty tough challenge. You’re driving past the McDonald’s and the Burger Kings and the Culvers and you’re thinking, Oh, wow, that looks great. And you shouldn’t go anywhere near it.

Sometimes you do. Sometimes you do because you decided you deserve a treat. Sometimes you do because you have no choice. My philosophy about that is, like anything in life, if you indulge, then you just have to pay the price on the other end. So that means having yogurt and granola for breakfast and some berries, and that means making sure you get to the gym.

I’m psychotic about the gym. In part because I have multiple sclerosis and I have some mobility challenges sometimes. At the end of just about every day, I get what the doctors call MS fatigue. You get headaches and your legs are very heavy. And so I have found in dealing with this that if I exercise in the morning, it really helps me. And so the other day, when we had that 6 a.m. flight, even though I didn’t get to bed until 11 at night, I got up at 2 in the morning and went to the hotel gym.

I’m trading sleep for exercise, which if you do that over 10 days, two weeks, you’re going to pay a price for it. But we’re doing five states in five days. It’s going to be pretty grueling anyway. We had an early start this morning. We had to be to a farm pretty early, and so I was at the hotel gym at 5:30 in the morning. That’s just part of my routine.

That depends on how much time I have. If I can, I work out for about 90 minutes in the morning. Every gym is a little different. Some hotels are great, some hotels are in-between. The hotel we stayed in last night was a bit of a time warp. The equipment was pretty old. If there’s a recumbent bike, I obviously have either emails from overnight to read or news articles to read or things to write. So I’ll spend 30 minutes or so on a recumbent bike, where I’m pedaling to get my body warmed up and I’m also doing some work, reading and communicating about the day ahead.

And then I get on the treadmill for a little bit. I’m not a runner, but I can jog a little bit, or do incline treadmill just to get my heart rate up a little bit, and then try to do a little bit of light weights if I have the time.

You do what you can. I’m pretty set in that I bike because I have to do some administrative stuff and that’s easiest on the bike. And then I get on the treadmill where I just try to listen to music and zone out a little bit. And if I can, I’ll do a quick circuit of some light weights because if you just do cardio, that one beer you have at the end of the night stays with you. So you got to do the weight.

I don’t usually write scripts or anything, but I will write to people back in Washington who are asking me questions. Or if I’m trying to find somebody on trips like this, a lot of stuff we do on the fly. I’ll occasionally write graphics. If I know I need to write a graphic or in the middle of a process, if we’re editing a piece, the editor might send me a graphic that they’ve done, What do you think? I’m not trying to write my actual scripts for pieces. Sometimes I tweak them, but if I tried to write them from scratch on a bike, I would lose my mind.

You have no choice. If I’m going to get my exercise in, at least part of that, it’s going to have to include some work time.

Yes. When I travel. I started this when I covered the White House—I covered the White House for 10 years—especially on international trips where you’re living on local time wherever you are in the world, but our CNN programming is on US time. I would have what I call the 20-minute rule where no matter how tired I was, if I was in a cool place around the world or even in the country, I just tried to get outside of the hotel for 20 minutes of me time. And so if you’re in Paris, you take a walk and stare at the Eiffel Tower.

I remember the Bush-Putin trip to Estonia where Bush said he looked into Putin’s soul. That became a big controversy. I remember after that day—we were on television all day and it was a big day—just walking around and looking at the architecture. The Berlin Wall had come down. We were a decade past that or more. But in a lot of those countries, you’d have this fabulous European architecture, like you’re in Paris or like you were in Prague, and then across the street would be this horrible concrete structure that the communists built.

And so that’s how I learned. I’m a kid who grew up in Dorchester, Massachusetts. My family had no money. We never traveled. So I have this enormous gift of this job that sends me everywhere. And so I really think it’s important both for the curiosity part of it, but also I have a lot of work to do, but I’ll actually be more efficient at my job if I take 20 minutes to just say, “Wow, this is a cool place. Let’s enjoy it.”

I don’t think of myself as someone who meditates, but do I sit still sometimes and listen to music. I try to keep up with the books my son in high school is reading. Sorry, CNN, sorry, politics, sorry, campaigns. I’m filing you away for 15 or 20 minutes. That’s absolutely critical to mental health.

I try to pack a carry-on on this trip because we’re out for five days. Plus, on the tail end of it, I have to go to New York City because my daughter lives in New York City and she just got engaged and we’re having a celebration for her on Saturday night.

Thank you. It’s a really amazing time. And of course, it all comes in a tornado, but that’s fine. But I have to bring a suit and I have to bring some other clothes. And as I said, my exercise is important, so I have to pack gym stuff. So usually I think of myself as a very efficient, tight packer so that I can have a carry-on bag, just so, number one, they can’t lose it. And number two, you can keep moving faster. But on this trip, I actually have to check my bag because I’m on the road for six days and then I’m going to New York for two more. I don’t like checking a bag, but so be it. I have to do it on this trip.

I operate on East Coast time all the time. I get tired. I wouldn’t really even call it jet lag because I try to keep my body on East Coast time and my brain on East Coast time because that’s who I report to. After international trips, I’ll get jet-lagged, but exercise is important, number one. I drink too much coffee, and so on a long trip, that can get to you. Your body gets a little jittery if you have a little bit of jet lag. You try to sleep when you can. One thing I was never good at until campaigns is napping. Now I can take a 20-minute nap. There was a time in my life I could not nap. I can take a 20-minute nap now, which helps you sometimes when you need to. But I’m just trying to think of the last time I had really profound jet lag. I can’t have jet lag, I guess.

Yeah. I’m not allowed. My work doesn’t allow me normally, so I just bull through it. That doesn’t mean I don’t get tired. This trip is going to be grueling. I’ll get to New York on Saturday and I’ll have three or four hours before my daughter’s dinner and I’ll need to get to the gym, but I’m also betting I’ll stare at a wall for a few minutes and just be like, Whoa. But I don’t dwell on it because I can’t.

It gets hard on the hotel menu. Most hotels now at least will have a yogurt parfait or at least yogurt. There’s a very wide—what do we want to call it?— quality control or quality between the different kind of hotels you stay at.

We’ve been to Wisconsin several times. There’s a hotel called The Trade in Wisconsin we always stay at and they have a spectacular yogurt granola parfait bowl. I know in the morning I’m going to have a nice, healthy breakfast. Other places, it’s a challenge and you can’t find it or you just have no choice. So you grab the bacon, egg and cheese sandwich and that means I’m having a salad for lunch.

Then when you’re on the road, like last night, we were driving here, we had a four-and-a-half-hour drive, so you stop at a random gas station in small town America and you’re a little hungry. I try to grab the almonds, not the potato chips. Luckily, I’ve never been a sugar person, so I’m not going to drink soda that has sugar in it. I don’t even really drink diet soda. But on the road, it’s mostly water and coffee. And then, I’d be lying if I didn’t say I’m very happy if I could find a cold beer at the end of the day.

Yesterday, we had fantastic Middle Eastern food in Dearborn, Michigan. Just a chicken salad, falafel. And we’ve been back there a couple times. There are a couple other places where we know of these small businesses, just some local person has started, just a place where they just have salads and healthy smoothies. When we’re in those towns, we go back to those places because we’re grateful they’re there and they help us reset the bad-road-food meter.

If I’m in Kansas City, I’m going to Arthur Bryant’s barbecue, and that is full of sodium and it’s not good for you, but it’s amazing.

Part of it, especially since my MS diagnosis, I know that I’m going to get tired. I may have issues with both my leg and my hand functions. You learn a lot more from your struggles than you do from your successes, and I’m much more aware of my body on a daily basis, even on a minute-to-minute basis of how I’m doing and what are my challenges at the moment. Hydration is critically important.

On election night, I might be standing for 16 hours. It’s probably closer to 12, but it might be 16. If you go back to 2020 when we had the election that went on all week, we didn’t call the election until Saturday. I was on my feet for 14 or 15 hours the first night, and then 12 hours the next day, and then 12 hours the day after that. That was a huge challenge.

That week was the longest. I’ve been on the road for campaigns covering candidates where it’s event, bus, presidential campaigns, you’re going from state to state. So it’s event, bus, plane, event, bus, plane, event, bus, plane. They’re handing you a box. You don’t even know what’s in it, but you eat it. Because it’s the only food you’re going to get for the next 10 hours.

In the studio, I’m standing on my feet the whole time, but I have access to cold water. Somebody can get me a coffee. If you’re on television, you’re just asking for it if you try to eat a salad or anything like that because it’s going to get in your teeth and you don’t have time to go down the hall. You just don’t. You’re on live television. So I get little tiny mini protein bars and put a few of them behind the Magic Wall. And if I feel like I just need a little energy boost, I’ll eat those. I drink more coffee than I should, but coffee will help me when I need a boost. And then when I’m done, I can go to sleep. I can have a Nespresso after dinner and go to bed. My colleagues hate me because of that.

When I am sometimes challenged by the MS issues I have, it’s when something surprising happens and I’m not prepared for it. And then an hour into having to do something that I didn’t know I was going to have to do, I might think, Wow, my legs are jello, or having, they call it MS brain. It’s like a foggy brain issue sometimes.

But I know the election is Tuesday. A lot of people ask me, “Why are you going on the road for five days? You don’t need to do that.” I do need to do it. Professionally, I need to do it. Physically, I will pay a price for this, but I know that. And so you just prepare for it.

The human brain is amazing. I don’t pretend to understand it, and MS has a lot of mysteries, but from when I was first diagnosed to now, I can prepare myself for something and I’ve been able to get through it, knock on wood, which is my skull.

I was diagnosed in 2008, and so we’ve had many big election nights since then, and I’ve gotten through them, and I’ll get through this next one. And then when it’s over, I will collapse. I’ll go home and I’ll fall into bed and I’ll sleep. But if I have to get up in four hours and do it again, I will. I’ve just trained myself to do that.

I work out a lot so that I stay fit physically and that I have good stamina. I’m 63 years young, as I like to say, so it’s important anyway that you stay more physically fit and more active in your body. Part of that is preparation.

In 2020, I was having issues with my hands, and my hands have to navigate a touchscreen Magic Wall. It’s hard for me to explain because you can’t see it, but the few people who have been around me when I’m having some struggles could see it. I have to watch more closely. I have to follow my hand because I can’t trust it to get where it’s going to go because it’s not connected to my brain.

I don’t know what’s in front of you right now, but if you have a notebook or a glass of water, you see it and you reach for it and then you stop looking. You don’t watch your hand anymore. You know where your hand’s going, your hand knows where it’s going. It picks up your phone. It starts typing on your keypad. Sometimes I have to watch my hands. I have to watch my hand pick it up, and then I have to check to make sure I have a good grip on it because I can’t feel my fingers.

I can’t feel the extremities. And so I will squeeze something extra tight. Sometimes, if you watch me on television, if my feet seem abnormally wide in my gait when I’m walking, that means I’m having balance issues and I spread my legs a little bit. To the naked eye, nobody sees that. If you’re around me all the time, you might say, “John’s walking a little weird today.”

MS is really cruel to some people. MS sucks for me. MS challenges me, but I have been able to manage it thanks to good doctors and thanks to personal discipline. I call it my visitor. If my visitor is active on any given day, my attitude is, okay, well, I can’t kick you out, so I have to figure out how to deal with you, and you just do it.

As much as I can. And then, if I have to come back at it the next day like I did in 2020, I was going home and getting three or four hours sleep, and maybe I could’ve had five or six hours sleep, but I know that I have to do that 45 minutes or 50 minutes of exercise to be able to function. So I have to cut my sleep short to get the exercise. That’s the way I have to do it to function. I’m able to get through it. Could I do that for a month? I hope I never have to answer that question. I was able to do it for a week in 2020. 2024, you’re still doing stuff the days after the election. We just didn’t have that long drawn out uncertainty.

I do not have trouble falling asleep. Even when I’m having a pretty good MS week, I have never had trouble sleeping. When my brain knows I’m done, I’m off the set, I’m in my office, I’ve had whatever post-action meeting I have to have, my brain tells me, “You’re done.” That means I’m going to find a bed, and I will sleep. I’ve been blessed so far, and I assume this will continue, that when I need to get back at it, I just get back at it.

Attitude is everything, especially if you’re tired or you’re struggling or things aren’t going well. Could I give you a list of complaints about my life? Could I give you a couple of complaints about where I work? Of course I could. Everybody can. As somebody who sometimes goes down to the gym in the basement of our office, why isn’t the office gym a little better? I mean, get over yourself. I think attitude is everything.

I say this as a sinner. When I was initially diagnosed, I was taking that out on other people sometimes. There were times when it was either the stress of work—this can be a stressful business sometimes—or the stress and the fear. I was being a grumpy person, not being a good colleague. If you feel that, take a walk, get away and just have a good attitude. In traveling the last two years, when you see the struggles that working families are going through across this country right now, I’ve always considered myself to be the luckiest person in the world. And when I feel myself starting to complain, I just give myself a whack in the head and say, “Dude, get over it.”

Attitude is incredibly important. That’s not a hack. It’s not a secret. It’s not a supplement, but look yourself in the mirror every morning and just go to it. Live your day in a way that you can look yourself in the mirror at the end of the day, and hold the gaze.

#6776. 9 Under Eye Wrinkle Treatments That Actually Work

Maybe you’re legitimately exhausted—or perhaps you just look it. Either way, an under eye wrinkle treatment can help. These formulations go a step beyond the your standard hydrating eye creams and under-eye patches to accomplish a near-impossible task: smoothing the crinkles and laugh lines around the eyes.

These lines can be especially tough to treat, according to Carmen Castilla, MD, board-certified dermatologist in New York, NY. For one, the skin in this area is “the thinnest on the face and is naturally more prone to wrinkling and accelerated aging,” she says. Years of smiling, laughing, or making any number of facial expressions can lead to deeper folds and wrinkles over time. And, because the skin here is more delicate, the eye area tends to be more prone to irritation—making it potentially harder to treat fine lines without setting skin off.

Because of that, not just any eye cream will do. Experts point to ingredients like retinoids, peptides, hyaluronic acid, and ceramides to smooth the look of wrinkles and give the area a fresher, tighter appearance. Still, keep in mind that a cream can only go so far. “While topicals can soften fine lines and improve texture, they will not tighten true laxity or deeper folds,” says Jane Yoo, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York. So you may want to consider it part of an overarching strategy for smoother, brighter eyes. With that in mind, here’s what to add to your top shelf.

Vogue’s Kiana Murden uses RoC’s Retinol Correxion Line Smoothing Eye Cream

What eye cream actually works for wrinkles?

An eye cream with targeted ingredients to spur collagen production—such as retinoids and peptides—can make the biggest difference in wrinkles around the eyes. However, early usage can make a world of difference in results, since lines around the eyes, being caused by facial expressions, only get worse over time. To that end, eye creams “are best for prevention and for patients with very fine lines,” Dr. Castilla says. “Once those lines are deep set, creams will make minimal impact.”

What to Look for in an Eye Cream for Wrinkles

Eye creams can be tough to navigate, in part because “everyone is looking for something a little different out of their creams,” says Erum Ilyas, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in King of Prussia, PA. “Some may be seeking support for dark undereye circles, others for puffiness, and others for wrinkles or heavy eyelids.”

Eye creams for wrinkles can also target these other concerns. Dr. Castilla points to retinoids in particular as a good ingredient to look for, as well as hydrators like glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and ceramides. These either “focus on either hydration of the surface of the skin to make it appear more supple and make wrinkles appear less apparent, or try to make the skin less pliable so it does not move as easily when the muscles are contracted,” says Dr. Ilyas.

Also important is what’s not in your eye cream. Since the skin around the eye is so fragile, “avoid alpha or beta hydroxy acids around the eyes for risks of skin sensitivity, and be careful with products containing fragrance,” says Dr. Ilyas.

Does anything actually help undereye wrinkles?

In addition to topical products like an eye cream, fillers or neurotoxin injections can go a long way. Ultimately crow’s-feet and undereye wrinkles “are the result of underlying muscular activity around the eyes that lends to squinting,” says Dr. Ilyas. “A cream won’t stop you from moving those muscles.” However, an injectable neuromodulator like Botox, Dysport, or Xeomin will.

Topicals alone won’t get rid of undereye wrinkles, but they’re a good start. The gold standard is a retinoid, which includes retinol, retinal, or prescription-strength tretinoin. “There is a plethora of clinical data to support their ability to stimulate collagen, accelerate cell turnover, and improve both fine lines and deeper wrinkles,” says Dr. Yoo, who suggests buffering the retinoid with a moisturizer since skin around the eye area is so easily irritated.

Other good options are peptides and growth factors. “Peptides consist of short chains or amino acids that can help with elasticity of the skin and help reduce wrinkles,” she says. “Growth factors are proteins that stimulate cell growth and repair.” These may not have the same kind of evidence behind them as retinoids, but they tend to be gentler in nature—making them an especially good option for getting rid of undereye wrinkles.

For faster results, hydrating ingredients can help, too. “Other ingredients, such as hyaluronic acid, give the skin an immediate plumping effect, which can reduce the appearance of fine lines,” says Dr. Yoo. And ceramides can soften the look of crepey skin and fine lines quickly, she adds. But again, topicals can only go so far—so pair these topical formulas with in-office treatments to get and maintain smoother, more youthful-looking eyes.

What in-office treatments achieve more intensive eye tightening?

There are a lot of in-office treatments that can help with undereye wrinkles and tighten skin. Let’s start with lasers. A fractional CO2 laser is the most powerful option out there, according to Dr. Yoo. “It resurfaces the skin and stimulates collagen,” she says, adding that it’s a good option for older patients who might not be surgical candidates.

Then, there are radiofrequency devices, like Thermage and Morpheus 8. “Radiofrequency devices deliver energy into the dermis to tighten and build collagen with less downtime,” Dr. Yoo says. The effects don’t last as long (roughly six to 12 months) so you’ll need to repeat the treatment for the best results.

And finally, you can consider ultrasound devices like Sofwave and Ultherapy, which “go a bit deeper than radiofrequency and target deeper tightening and brow lifting,” says Dr. Yoo. “You can see the peak effect at around the two to three month period, with results lasting up to a year.” That said, there’s a limit to even what non-invasive treatments can achieve. “If you have excess skin or prominent eye bags, "a surgical consultation may be more appropriate," she says.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to under-eye wrinkle treatments, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, finish, and the skin-care concerns they address (from hollowness to creases to ‌undereye bags). To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you.
